title: Part 2, Chapter 33
paragraphs: About the delightful discourse the duchess and her damsels had with Sancho Panza, well worth reading and noting

The history records that Sancho did not sleep that afternoon but, in order to keep his word, came to visit the duchess before he had quite finished dinner. She, finding enjoyment in listening to him, made him sit down beside her on a low seat, although Sancho, out of pure good breeding, didn't want to sit down; the duchess, however, told him he was to sit down as a governor and talk as a squire, since in both respects he was worthy of even the chair of the Cid Ruy Diaz the Campeador. Sancho shrugged his shoulders, obeyed, and sat down, and all the duchess's damsels and duennas gathered around him, waiting in profound silence to hear what he would say. It was the duchess, however, who spoke first, saying:

"Now that we are alone, and there is nobody here to overhear us, I should be glad if the señor governor would relieve me of certain doubts I have, arising out of the history of the great Don Quixote that is now in print. One is: given that worthy Sancho never saw Dulcinea — I mean the lady Dulcinea del Toboso — nor took Don Quixote's letter to her, since it was left in the notebook in the Sierra Morena, how did he dare to invent the answer and all that business about finding her sifting wheat, the whole story being a deception and a lie, and so much to the prejudice of the peerless Dulcinea's good name — a thing not at all becoming the character and fidelity of a good squire?"

At these words Sancho, without uttering one in reply, got up from his chair, and with noiseless steps, his body bent and his finger on his lips, he went all round the room lifting up the wall-hangings. This done, he came back to his seat and said, "Now, señora, that I've seen there's no one but the bystanders listening to us on the sly, I'll answer what you've asked me, and anything else you may ask me, without fear or dread. The first thing I have to say is that for my own part I take my master Don Quixote to be stark mad, though sometimes he says things that to my mind, and to everybody's who listens to him, are so wise and run in such a straight furrow that Satan himself could not have said them better. But for all that, really and truly, it's my firm belief that he is cracked. Well then, since this is clear to me, I can risk making him believe things that have neither head nor tail, like that business of the answer to the letter, and that other business of six or eight days ago which isn't yet in any history — I mean the business of the enchantment of my lady Dulcinea. I made him believe she's enchanted, when there's no more truth in it than over the hills of Úbeda."

The duchess begged him to tell her about the enchantment or deception, so Sancho told the whole story exactly as it had happened, and his hearers were not a little amused by it. Then resuming, the duchess said, "In consequence of what worthy Sancho has told me, a doubt starts up in my mind, and there comes a kind of whisper to my ear that says, 'If Don Quixote is mad, crazy, and cracked, and Sancho Panza his squire knows it, and nevertheless serves and follows him, and goes on trusting to his empty promises, there can be no doubt that he must be still madder and sillier than his master; and that being so, it will be cast in your teeth, señora duchess, if you give the said Sancho an island to govern — because how will he who doesn't know how to govern himself know how to govern others?'"

"By God, señora," said Sancho, "that doubt comes at just the right time. Your grace may say it straight out and speak plainly, or however you like, because I know what you say is true; if I were wise, I'd have left my master long ago. But this was my fate, this was my bad luck; I can't help it, I have to follow him. We're from the same village, I've eaten his bread, I'm fond of him, I'm grateful, he gave me his ass-colts, and above all I'm faithful; so it's quite impossible for anything to separate us except the pickaxe and shovel. And if your highness doesn't care to give me the government you promised, God made me without it, and maybe your not giving it to me will be all the better for my conscience — because fool as I am, I know the proverb 'to her hurt the ant got wings,' and it may be that Sancho the squire will get to heaven sooner than Sancho the governor. 'They make as good bread here as in France,' and 'by night all cats are grey,' and 'a hard case enough is his who hasn't broken his fast by two in the afternoon,' and 'there's no stomach a hand's breadth bigger than another,' and the same can be filled 'with straw or hay,' as the saying goes, and 'the little birds of the field have God for their purveyor and caterer,' and 'four yards of Cuenca frieze keep one warmer than four of Segovia broadcloth,' and 'when we quit this world and are put underground the prince travels by as narrow a path as the journeyman,' and 'the Pope's body takes up no more feet of earth than the sacristan's,' for all that the one stands higher than the other; because when we go to our graves we all pack ourselves up and make ourselves small, or rather they pack us up and make us small in spite of ourselves, and then — good night to us. And I say once more: if your ladyship doesn't care to give me the island because I'm a fool, like a wise man I'll take care not to trouble myself about it. I've heard say that 'behind the cross there's the devil,' and that 'all that glitters is not gold,' and that from among the oxen and the ploughs and the yokes, Wamba the husbandman was taken to be made King of Spain, and from among brocades and pleasures and riches, Roderick was taken to be devoured by adders — if the verses of the old ballads don't lie."

"To be sure they don't lie!" exclaimed Doña Rodriguez, the duenna, who was one of the listeners. "There's a ballad that says they put King Rodrigo alive into a tomb full of toads, and adders, and lizards, and that two days afterwards the king, in a plaintive, feeble voice, cried out from inside the tomb—
They gnaw me now, they gnaw me now, There where I most did sin.
And according to that, the gentleman has good reason to say he'd rather be a labouring man than a king, if vermin are going to eat him."

The duchess could not help laughing at the simplicity of her duenna, or wondering at the language and proverbs of Sancho, to whom she said, "Worthy Sancho knows very well that when once a knight has made a promise, he strives to keep it, even if it should cost him his life. My lord and husband the duke, though not one of the errant sort, is none the less a knight for that reason, and will keep his word about the promised island, in spite of the envy and malice of the world. Let Sancho be of good cheer; when he least expects it he'll find himself seated on the throne of his island and seat of dignity, and will take possession of his government — only to discard it for another of three-bordered brocade. The charge I give him is to be careful how he governs his vassals, bearing in mind that they are all loyal and well-born."

"As for governing them well," said Sancho, "there's no need to charge me to do that, because I'm kind-hearted by nature and full of compassion for the poor. 'There's no stealing the loaf from him who kneads and bakes,' and by my faith it won't do to throw false dice with me; I'm an old dog, and I know all about 'tus, tus.' I can be wide awake when need be, and I don't let clouds come before my eyes, because I know where the shoe pinches me. I say so because with me the good will have support and protection, and the bad neither footing nor entry. And it seems to me that in governments, to make a beginning is everything; and perhaps, after being governor for a fortnight, I'll take to the work and know more about it than the field labour I was brought up to."

"You are right, Sancho," said the duchess, "because no one is born ready taught, and bishops are made out of men, not out of stones. But to return to the subject we were discussing just now, the enchantment of the lady Dulcinea: I look upon it as certain, and more than evident, that Sancho's idea of practising a deception on his master — making him believe the peasant girl was Dulcinea and that if he didn't recognise her it must be because she was enchanted — was all the work of one of the enchanters who persecute Don Quixote. Because in truth and earnest, I know from good authority that the coarse country wench who jumped up on the donkey was and is Dulcinea del Toboso, and that worthy Sancho, though he fancies himself the deceiver, is the one who's been deceived; and there's no more reason to doubt the truth of this than of anything else we never saw. Señor Sancho Panza must know that we too have enchanters here who are well disposed to us, and tell us what goes on in the world plainly and distinctly, without subterfuge or deception. And believe me, Sancho, that nimble country lass was and is Dulcinea del Toboso, who is just as enchanted as the mother that bore her; and when we least expect it, we shall see her in her own proper form, and then Sancho will be undeceived of the error he is under now."

"That's all quite possible," said Sancho Panza. "And now I'm willing to believe what my master says about what he saw in the cave of Montesinos, where he says he saw the lady Dulcinea del Toboso in the very same dress and apparel I said I had seen her in when I enchanted her purely to please myself. It must be the other way round, as your ladyship says, because it's impossible to suppose that out of my poor wit such a cunning trick could be cooked up in a moment, nor do I think my master is so mad that by my weak and feeble persuasion he could be made to believe a thing so out of all reason. But, señora, your excellency must not therefore think me ill-disposed, because a dolt like me isn't bound to see into the thoughts and plots of those vile enchanters. I invented all that to escape my master's scolding, not with any intention of hurting him; and if it has turned out differently, there is a God in heaven who judges our hearts."
"That is true," said the duchess. "But tell me, Sancho, what is this you say about the cave of Montesinos? I'd like to know."

Sancho thereupon related to her, word for word, what has already been said about that adventure, and having heard it the duchess said, "From this incident it may be inferred that, since the great Don Quixote says he saw there the same country wench Sancho saw on the way from El Toboso, it is no doubt Dulcinea, and that there are some very active and exceedingly busy enchanters about."

"So I say," said Sancho, "and if my lady Dulcinea is enchanted, so much the worse for her; I'm not going to pick a quarrel with my master's enemies, who seem to be many and spiteful. The truth is that the one I saw was a country wench, and I took her for a country wench; and if that was Dulcinea it must not be laid at my door, nor should I be called to answer for it or take the consequences. But they have to keep nagging at me at every turn — 'Sancho said it, Sancho did it, Sancho here, Sancho there,' as if Sancho was nobody at all, and not that same Sancho Panza who's now going all over the world in books, so Samson Carrasco told me; and he is at least a bachelor of Salamanca, and people of that sort can't lie, except when the whim takes them or they have some very good reason for it. So there's no occasion for anyone to quarrel with me; and besides, I have a good character, and as I've heard my master say, 'a good name is better than great riches.' Just stick me into this government and they'll see wonders, because one who's been a good squire will be a good governor."

"All worthy Sancho's observations," said the duchess, "are Catonian maxims, or at any rate straight out of the very heart of Michael Verino himself, who _florentibus occidit annis_. In fact, to speak in his own style, 'under a bad cloak there's often a good drinker.'"

"Indeed, señora," said Sancho, "I never yet drank out of wickedness; from thirst very likely, because I have nothing of the hypocrite in me. I drink when I'm inclined, or if I'm not inclined, when they offer it to me, so as not to look either strait-laced or ill-bred — because when a friend drinks to your health, what heart can be so hard as not to return it? But if I put on my shoes I don't dirty them. Besides, squires to knights-errant mostly drink water, because they're always wandering among woods, forests and meadows, mountains and crags, without a drop of wine to be had if they gave their eyes for it."
"So I believe," said the duchess. "And now let Sancho go take his sleep, and we'll talk later at greater length, and settle how he may soon go and stick himself into the government, as he says."
Sancho once more kissed the duchess's hand and begged her to let good care be taken of his Dapple, for he was the light of his eyes.
"What is Dapple?" said the duchess.

"My donkey," said Sancho, "which, so as not to call him by that name, I'm accustomed to call Dapple. I begged this lady duenna here to take care of him when I came into the castle, and she got as angry as if I'd called her ugly or old — though it ought to be more natural and proper for duennas to feed donkeys than to ornament chambers. God bless me, what a grudge a gentleman of my village had against these ladies!"
"He must have been some clown," said Doña Rodriguez the duenna; "because if he'd been a gentleman and well-born, he would have exalted them higher than the horns of the moon."

"That'll do," said the duchess; "no more of this. Hush, Doña Rodriguez, and let Señor Panza rest easy and leave the treatment of Dapple to me, because since he is a treasure of Sancho's, I'll set him on the apple of my eye."

"It'll be enough for him to be in the stable," said Sancho, "because neither he nor I are worthy to rest a moment on the apple of your highness's eye, and I'd as soon stab myself as consent to it; for although my master says that in matters of civility it's better to lose by a card too many than a card too few, when it comes to civilities to donkeys we have to watch what we're about and keep within proper bounds."
"Take him to your government, Sancho," said the duchess, "and there you'll be able to make as much of him as you like, and even release him from work and pension him off."
"Don't think, señora duchess, that you've said anything absurd," said Sancho. "I've seen more than two donkeys go to governments, so for me to take mine with me would be nothing new."

Sancho's words made the duchess laugh again and gave her fresh amusement, and dismissing him to sleep she went off to tell the duke the conversation she'd had with him. Between them they plotted and arranged to play a joke on Don Quixote that was to be a rare one and entirely in knight-errantry style, and in that same style they pulled off several more on him, so much in keeping and so cleverly done that they form the best adventures this great history contains.
